items.prompt: Why does "any feedback?" tend to produce vague answers like "looks good," even from people who genuinely have real opinions?
choices: Because people are usually dishonest when asked for feedback

A vague, open-ended question makes a vague answer the easiest, lowest-risk response available — it's not that there's nothing to say, it's that the question doesn't require anything specific to be said
Because "looks good" is always factually false in these situations
Because most people don't actually read what they're asked to review
items.explanation: The vague default isn't necessarily dishonesty — it's the natural equilibrium of a question with no specific target. A vague answer to a vague question costs no effort and carries no social risk, which is exactly what a narrower question closes off.
items.reference:
Vague question

No specific target → vague answer costs nothing

Specific question

A named target → a vague answer looks like skipping it

Why: the question's shape decides how easy a low-effort answer is, independent of how much the person actually has to say.
items.learnMore:
The path of least resistance

Every question implicitly sets a bar for what counts as a complete answer. "Any feedback?" sets that bar at almost nothing — "looks good" satisfies it fully, so that's what most people default to, regardless of what they actually noticed.

This isn't about honesty. Someone can genuinely believe "looks good" is true in the moment and still be leaving real, useful observations unsaid, simply because nothing in the question invited them.

Common mistake

Concluding that a vague answer means there was nothing to say. It usually just means nothing was asked for.

That the coworker didn't have time to look at it at all
items.explanation: A generic answer to a generic question is uninformative by construction — it's the easiest true-ish response available regardless of what the person actually noticed, so it can't be used to distinguish a clean bill of health from a question that never asked for anything specific.

items.prompt: Per L1, why does asking "how's the pricing slide specifically?" tend to produce more useful feedback than "any feedback on this deck?"
choices: Because it's a shorter question, and shorter questions are always answered more carefully

Because a specific question closes off the easy vague-answer exit — plausibly answering it with "looks good" would itself read as having skipped the slide, making a real answer the new path of least resistance
Because pricing slides are inherently more interesting than other parts of a deck
There's no real difference; question phrasing doesn't affect answer quality
items.explanation: The mechanism is about what counts as an easy, low-risk answer. A specific question makes a generic response implausible as a complete answer, which pushes the respondent toward giving genuinely specific, useful feedback instead.
items.reference:
🗣️ "Any feedback?" → easy to answer with nothing
🎯 "How's the pricing slide?" → forces a real answer

Why: narrowing the question doesn't limit the feedback — it removes the safe, generic exit.
items.learnMore:
Narrowing as a forcing function

A narrow question doesn't restrict what someone can say — it removes their easiest way of saying nothing. "How's the pricing slide" still allows any answer, including "it's fine," but that answer now has to be about the pricing slide specifically, which most people won't claim unless they actually looked.

This is why scoping to one part of the work usually outperforms asking about the whole thing at once — the whole-thing version has too many places to hide a non-answer.

Common mistake

Assuming a narrow question limits how much feedback you can get. It's the opposite — it's what makes a full answer likely in the first place.

items.prompt: Two coworkers review the same deck. One is asked "any feedback?", the other "how's the pricing slide?". Both spend the exact same five minutes reading. Which is more likely to surface something Maya can actually act on, and why?

Neither — the amount of time spent reading is what determines feedback quality, not the question
The "how's the pricing slide?" version — the same five minutes of attention gets pointed at something specific, instead of being free to settle on the easiest thing to say about the whole deck
They're equally likely; question phrasing has no bearing on outcome
items.explanation: Given equal attention, a narrow question directs where that attention lands and what a complete answer has to address. The same five minutes produces a specific finding under a narrow question and often just a general impression under a broad one.

items.prompt: Per L1, what does "calibration" mean in the context of asking for feedback?
choices: Making sure your question is grammatically precise
Knowing how much weight to put on a given piece of feedback, since the same words from different people (or the same person on different days) can carry very different amounts of real signal
Asking exactly the same question every time so answers can be compared
A formal performance-review process run once a year
items.explanation: Calibration is about interpreting the answer you got, not about the question's wording or a formal process — it's the separate skill of figuring out how much trust a given piece of feedback deserves.
items.reference:
Same words ("looks good") from a careful reader vs. a skimmer carry very different amounts of real signal.

Why: calibration asks "how much should I trust this answer," a separate question from "what did the answer say."
items.learnMore:
Calibration is a second skill, not a rewording of the first

Getting a specific answer (via a narrow question) and knowing how much to trust that answer are two different problems. A specific answer can still come from someone who barely looked — calibration is what catches that.

The simplest calibration tool is a direct follow-up: "did you read the whole thing, or just this part?" It costs almost nothing to ask and tells you exactly how far the feedback's coverage extends.

Common mistake

Treating every "looks good" as equally meaningful regardless of who said it or how much they engaged.

items.prompt: Two reviewers both say "looks good" about the same document. One reads every line carefully; the other skims. Per L1's idea of calibration, what should you do with these two answers?
choices: Treat them identically, since they said the same words
Discard the skimmer's opinion entirely as worthless
Weight them differently, since the same words carry different amounts of real signal depending on how carefully each person actually engaged
Assume the careful reader is always right and the skimmer is always wrong
items.explanation: Calibration means recognizing that identical words can carry very different amounts of signal depending on engagement — not discarding one opinion, and not assuming either reviewer is objectively "right," just weighting each appropriately.

items.prompt: Per L1, why can psychological safety matter more than the exact wording of a feedback question?
choices: It doesn't — wording is the only thing that matters

Because someone who believes candid criticism will be held against them tends to give safer, vaguer answers no matter how the question is phrased — safety is a property of the relationship, not just the question
Because psychological safety is only relevant in formal performance reviews
Because safety only matters for junior employees, not peers
items.explanation: A well-phrased question increases the odds of a real answer, but it doesn't override a well-founded fear that candor carries a cost — that fear is rooted in the relationship and environment, not fixable by rewording alone.
items.reference:
A perfectly narrow question still gets a safe answer if the person doesn't trust that candor is welcome.

Why: safety is a precondition question phrasing works on top of, not a substitute for it.
items.learnMore:
Safety as the ground, not a step

Question phrasing and psychological safety solve different problems. Phrasing removes the easy, generic exit; safety removes the incentive to avoid candor in the first place. You need both — a narrow question asked in an unsafe relationship just gets a narrow, safe answer instead of a broad, safe one.

Building safety is mostly about what happens after someone gives candid feedback: whether it's received well, acted on, and never held against them later.

Common mistake

Assuming a perfectly worded question is enough on its own, regardless of the relationship it's asked inside.

Phrasing and safety are unrelated, so this scenario can't be predicted
items.explanation: Good phrasing removes the easy vague exit, but if candor has previously carried a real cost, the safer default reappears — safety and phrasing are two separate, necessary conditions, not substitutes.

items.prompt: Per L1, why does asking about a specific, finished piece of work tend to beat asking a broad question like "how am I doing"?
choices: Because finished work is always higher quality than ongoing work
Broad questions can't be answered from any single memory, so they collapse into a general impression — a specific, recent, finished thing gives the person an actual event to reference
Because "how am I doing" is considered rude in most workplaces
There's no real difference between the two kinds of questions
items.explanation: The scope principle mirrors the phrasing principle: a broad question has nothing specific to anchor an answer to, so it collapses into a vague aggregate impression, while a specific, recent thing gives a concrete event to reference.
items.reference:
Broad, ongoing

"How am I doing?" → no single memory to anchor to

Specific, finished

"How did Tuesday's call go?" → one checkable event
items.learnMore:
Scope is the same principle as phrasing, applied differently

Narrow phrasing closes off a vague answer to a specific question. Narrow scope does the same thing to a specific event — "how am I doing overall" has no single moment to check against, so it invites a general, hard-to-verify impression instead of a real answer.

Picking something recent and finished (a call, a draft, a decision) gives the other person a concrete thing to remember and evaluate, rather than asking them to summarize an aggregate on the spot.

Common mistake

Saving all feedback-seeking for a single broad, scheduled check-in instead of asking about specific recent things as they happen.

items.prompt: What's the trap L1 warns about regarding feedback-seeking as a "one-time event"?

That feedback should only ever be given in writing
That one-time feedback is always more accurate than ongoing feedback
items.explanation: The trap isn't about the format of reviews — it's about the cost of delay. Treating feedback as a scheduled event rather than an ongoing habit means real, fixable issues go unaddressed for far longer than necessary.

items.prompt: Per L2, why doesn't "looks good!" from a vague question necessarily mean the person is lying?
choices: Because "looks good" is always technically true
Because it's the natural equilibrium of a question that requires nothing specific — a vague answer costs no effort and carries no social risk, so it's the default outcome, not evidence of dishonesty
Because most people can't tell the difference between good and bad work
Because feedback is always subjective, so no answer can be "wrong"
items.explanation: L2 frames the vague default as an equilibrium effect of question shape, not a character judgment — the same person would likely give a real answer if the question closed off the easy exit.
items.reference:
Vague ask

Easiest honest-enough answer → "looks good"

Narrow ask

Vague answer implausible → forces a real one
items.learnMore:
Equilibrium, not character

A vague question sets a very low bar for what counts as a satisfying answer. Most people, most of the time, will meet that bar exactly and no further — not because they're being evasive, but because meeting it costs nothing and going further isn't asked for.

A specific question raises that bar: a generic answer to "how's the pricing slide" would visibly fail to address what was asked, so the same person who gave a vague answer before now gives a real one.

Common mistake

Reading a vague answer as a character flaw in the person giving it, rather than a predictable response to a vague question.

items.prompt: Per L2's calibration table, which signal suggests feedback deserves to be weighted heavily?
choices: The response arrived very quickly
The response used generic, non-specific language
The response referenced specific, actual content (e.g. a specific line or slide)
The response agreed with what you already believed
items.explanation: Specific references to actual content are the clearest sign of genuine engagement — the other options (speed, agreement, genericness) are each explicitly called out as things that warrant a closer look, not automatic trust.
items.reference:
SignalSuggests
Specific reference to contentHigh engagement

items.learnMore:
Reading the signals, not just the words

Calibration works by looking past the literal content of the answer to how it was produced: what it references, how quickly it arrived, and whether it matches this person's track record.

None of these signals is proof on its own — a fast response can still be from someone with excellent instincts. They're inputs to a judgment call, not a formula.

Common mistake

Treating speed of response as a reliable proxy for how carefully something was reviewed.

items.prompt: In L2's four-step decision procedure, where does psychological safety fit?
choices: It's the fifth and final step, applied after the other four
It isn't part of the procedure at all
It's the precondition underneath all four steps — none of the four steps rescues a question asked where candor isn't safe
It replaces the need for a calibration follow-up
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that psychological safety sits underneath the four-step procedure as a precondition, not as one more step in the sequence — a perfectly executed procedure still fails without it.
items.reference: Scope → narrow → ask the right person → calibrate — all four sit on top of psychological safety, not alongside it as a fifth step.
items.learnMore:
Ground vs. steps

A procedure with sequential steps implies each step is roughly independent and addable. Psychological safety isn't like that — it's more like the ground the other four steps stand on. Remove it, and the other four steps don't fail one at a time; they all fail together, because the underlying willingness to be candid is gone.

This is why L2 places it below the flowchart rather than as a fifth box inside it.

Common mistake

Treating safety as just another box to check in the sequence, rather than the thing the whole sequence depends on.

items.prompt: Per L2's decision-procedure flowchart, when should you add a calibration follow-up like "did you read it all?"
choices: Always, after every single piece of feedback, regardless of how it sounds
Never — calibration follow-ups are redundant once a specific question has been asked
When the first answer sounds too smooth or complete for how much time/attention was likely available
Only during formal annual reviews
items.explanation: The flowchart's branch is conditional: if the answer sounds too smooth given the likely attention available, add the calibration follow-up; if it's already clearly specific and grounded, trust it proportionally instead.
items.reference: Pick something recent + finished → narrow it → ask someone whose answer you'll weight → if the answer sounds too smooth, add a calibration follow-up.
items.learnMore:
The procedure is conditional, not a fixed script

L2's four-step flow isn't "always do all four in order no matter what" — the calibration follow-up is specifically gated on whether the first answer already seems earned or seems too easy given the circumstances.

items.prompt: Per L3's failure modes, what's the difference between "how's the pricing slide?" and "why didn't you catch the pricing gap, don't you usually review carefully?"

items.learnMore:
Interrogating the person vs. examining the work

A question aimed at the work ("how's the pricing slide") invites the reviewer to talk about the deck. A question aimed at the reviewer's diligence ("don't you usually review carefully") invites them to defend themselves — a completely different, much less comfortable task.

The same specificity that makes a question useful can be aimed at either target — the goal is always the work, never the reviewer's competence.

Common mistake

Confusing "specific" with "pointed at the person" — specificity should target the work, not the reviewer.
